answer.sourceLine: Sowell wrote this exact sentence as one item in his syndicated “Random thoughts” column of May 1, 2007 (Creators Syndicate). National Review Online ran the column as “Don’t Get Weak”, and Townhall and Jewish World Review ran it as “Random thoughts”. All three archived copies contain the wording word for word.

source.excerpt: When I see the worsening degeneracy in our politicians, our media, our educators, and our intelligentsia, I can’t help wondering if the day may yet come when the only thing that can save this country is a military coup.
trail: May 1, 2007: Sowell’s Creators Syndicate column ran on National Review Online as “Don’t Get Weak” ↗, with the sentence word for word and a © 2007 Creators Syndicate line.
Same column, other outlets: Townhall ↗ and Jewish World Review ↗ both ran it as “Random thoughts”, dated May 1, 2007, with identical wording.

May 2, 2007: bloggers picked up the line straight away. James Joyner’s post at Outside the Beltway ↗ and Daniel Larison’s at The American Conservative ↗ both quoted it and linked to the National Review column.
Wikiquote: the Thomas Sowell page ↗ lists the line among its sourced quotes and cites “Don’t Get Weak”, National Review, May 1, 2007.
source.excerptNote: This is one stand-alone item in a list of unconnected one-line “random thoughts”. It comes right after a quip about Suze Orman and before an item about Alan Reynolds’s book Income and Wealth. Earlier in the same column, another item complains that “our education system, our media, and our intelligentsia” have been undermining the country’s values for generations.

author.bio: Thomas Sowell was born in Gastonia, North Carolina, in 1930. He is an economist and social theorist and has been a senior fellow at Stanford’s Hoover Institution since 1977. For decades he wrote a nationally syndicated column for Creators Syndicate, including the recurring “Random thoughts on the passing scene” feature, which was a list of short one-line items. He announced the end of the column in December 2016.

context.heading: Why it drew fire
lead: The line was one of a couple of dozen unconnected one-liners in a routine “Random thoughts” column. Other items in the same column joked about Suze Orman and Babe Ruth’s World Series record. Because it sat in a list, nothing in the column itself explains it or adds a caveat, and that left readers to decide how literally Sowell meant it.

The reaction came the next day. At Outside the Beltway, James Joyner’s post was titled “Thomas Sowell Pines for A Military Coup” ↗. At The American Conservative, Daniel Larison asked “Sowell Calls For Bush’s Overthrow?” ↗ Since then the sentence has circulated mostly as a stand-alone quotation, with no sign that it was one item in a list.
